paragraphs.text: The prophets proclaim the gospel of Christ's kingdom, the ministers of the new grace interpret it, and those who hear, love and praise the divine word receive it. No one can delight in the word of truth who does not thirst for the word of teaching. Just as no one can enjoy food with pleasure who is not thirsty and hungry, so no one can delight in the word of truth who does not thirst for the teaching of the Holy Spirit. That is why the Savior says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled." The true food of souls, the true delight of the godly, the true wealth of the godly is the word of God, which speaks through David. At one time he glories in it as one who is rich, at another as one who feasts, and he says: "How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" Here he spoke as one who feasts, for the word of God was his delight. Of this he often said: "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart." Elsewhere he prides himself on the wealth of the law, not only as one who feasts but also as one who is rich, saying: "The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces." Do you see the delight of godliness and the wealth that lies in righteousness? We must therefore thirst for divine things and hunger for heavenly things, and enjoy an abundant feast from Christ's royal table. We must also hold fast to the gospel of salvation, which did not begin just now but was founded in the prophets and built up in the apostles. For the gospel did not begin when Christ appeared. It was rooted in the books of the prophets and blossomed in the preaching of the apostles. That is why Paul, wanting to show that the gospel did not begin with the incarnation but shone out from the prophets, proclaims it by way of the incarnation: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh." Paul knows that the old covenant and the new are undivided. That is why he sometimes calls it the new covenant, to show how the ends of the earth were made new. I know that I dealt with this subject recently, but I repeat it as a reminder. He calls it the new covenant, then, in contrast to the one that had grown old; the better covenant in contrast to the lesser; the eternal covenant in contrast to the temporary one. He also calls it the second covenant. Why second? To link the two in our minds. For what is cut off from something is not called its second. But since God spoke both in the first and in the second, the same Paul calls them first and second, using the numbering to bring out their agreement. That is why Paul, proclaiming the undivided kingdom of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, sometimes calls the gospel that of God the Father and sometimes that of the Son. He says: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God." But so that no one hearing "gospel of God" should think that the Son has no authority over the preaching, a little further on in the same letter he says: "For God, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, is my witness." Do you see how wonderful this herald is, and how finely ordered his mind? So that no one would think he served one God under the law and went over to another in the gospel, he says: "Blessed be God, whom I serve with a clean conscience, as my forefathers did." "I did not run from one God to another," he means; "the God I had in ignorance I took up in knowledge." Again, wanting to show that the words of the old covenant and the new come from one mouth and one Master, he cited a single testimony from Scripture, weaving the old into the gospel saying: "It is written: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain, and the worker deserves his wages." "You shall not muzzle" was said by Moses; "the worker deserves his wages" was said by Christ in the Gospels. But to show that one mouth spoke both, he joined what was separated in time in the harmony of truth, saying: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain, and the worker deserves his wages." An image of this gospel is Peter's nets, let down today before our eyes and in our hearing. For Peter did not let down the nets only once. In the historical event it was once, but in its power it is many times. Whenever the gospel is preached, I see nothing else but Peter and Andrew and the company of the apostles spreading out the net of the gospel.

It was a strange sight to see the Savior on the sea and those being taught standing on the shore. A strange thing: the fish on the land and the fisherman on the sea! The casting of that net was an image of the word of the gospel. He found the fishermen, it says, washing their nets, as men who had given up on the catch. For a fisherman does not wash his net unless he has given up fishing. So the Savior found them after they had given up on the catch, and the Master of the catch comes to them. And what does he do? First he teaches the word of truth, then he orders the net to be let down. Since words without deeds were unproven, proof by deeds had to follow the word, to show that when God commands, even what cannot be found is caught and what does not exist is taken. "Let down your net," he says. And Peter says: "Master, we toiled all night and caught nothing, but at your word I will let down the net." I admire Peter's faith: he gave up on what came before and believed in what was new. "At your word I will let down the net." Why did he say "at your word"? Because at his word the heaven was made firm, the earth was founded, the sea was given its bounds, the earth was crowned with its own flowers, and all things hold together by your word, as Paul says: "upholding all things by the word of his power." "But at your word I will let down the net." The word went down ahead of the net. The fish are not there; and even if they had been, they would have fled because of the commotion of the fishermen. But the word of him who calls the things that are not as though they were went down. The power of the one who gave the command went down ahead of the net. A multitude of fish was gathered—it was an image of the universal Church. The net was breaking; they signaled to their partners' boat to come and help them. For two boats had to work together for the catch. Unless the company of the prophets is there to help the apostles' hand, and unless the work of the apostles follows on the prophets' prediction, the catch is not taken. So the Savior, wanting to show that the catch of fish is an image of the Church, and wanting to train Peter further by this example, anointed him for courage and says to him: "Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching people alive." "From now on," he means, "since you have experienced my power and learned that even creatures without reason obey the Word, and that all things follow my nod. You have received a sufficient example; now take up the catch." And he did not say, "You will be fishing for people," but "You will be catching people alive." For fish are caught from life into death, but people are caught from death into life. "From now on," he says, "you will be catching people alive." Why then does he say to him, "Do not be afraid"? Granted, the promise looked fair. Why then "do not be afraid"? Because Peter had fallen to remembering his former sins. "Do not be afraid for yourself as a sinner," he says, "but from now on think of yourself as an apostle, commanded by your Master's word to cast your net over the world." "Do not be afraid"—let every sinner hear this from Christ: "Do not be afraid." Only let him repent from now on. The net, then—to return to my earlier train of thought—is an image of the Savior's gospel teaching. And Paul calls this gospel sometimes the gospel of righteousness, sometimes the gospel of peace, and sometimes the gospel of power. For the grace of the preaching has the power both to abolish wars and to scatter the factions of people who do not agree in godliness. Because it calls all to salvation, it is called the gospel of righteousness; because it puts down the war of the demons, it is called the gospel of peace; because it proclaims the knowledge of God in plain words, it is called the gospel of power. Listen to Paul saying: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation." For what is powerful is shown to be powerful when it conquers the ends of the earth without making use of reasoned arguments, as the Savior says to Paul: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." It would have been nothing great if he had enlightened the world with his naked Godhead; what is great is that he displayed his impassible and incorporeal glory through a body. It would have been nothing wonderful if the Living One had given life to the world by flashing out his life-giving glory; the power of the Word lies in this, that he abolishes death by death and makes his immortal glory shine out through insults. Elsewhere Paul says "the gospel of peace": "Make your feet ready," he says, "with the readiness of the gospel of peace." Elsewhere he calls it the gospel of righteousness, as when he says: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for in it the righteousness of God is revealed." What is "the righteousness of God"? Since the first law was given to the Jews alone but the gospel to all, he calls it the gospel of righteousness. For God is just: having made all alike, he enlightened all alike. And this was just: not to save some and not others, not to call some and not others. In the old covenant the calling was not just, but a provisional arrangement preparing the way for righteousness. I do not say that this covenant is just and that one unjust, but that the old one is the way to the new and its preparation. He gave the law to Israel, and David says: "He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so for any other nation, and he has not shown them his judgments."

So whereas he revealed the old covenant to one nation, here he weighed out the word of truth in the balance and mixed it in equal measure for all. Pay attention, I beg you. Righteousness means saving all alike, with no difference between slave and free, barbarian or Greek, woman or man. As Paul says: "In Christ Jesus there is neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither male nor female, neither slave nor free." Do you see the equality of honor? Since our nature is equal in honor, even though we have been divided by our choices, he gathers our nature back to its original beauty. For when Adam was formed, there was no foreigner, no Scythian, no barbarian, no Greek, no slave, no free, no male, no female; from the one he brought forth the two. Nature did not beget slavery; choice gave birth to it. There is also forced slavery, which comes from the misfortune of famine or the compulsion of captivity. And there is another, voluntary slavery, which sells its own freedom by marrying slave women and comes under the yoke of slavery. But the first slavery arose from an evil disposition. Hear where the root of slavery is found. After the flood Noah drank wine, and because he was inexperienced and did not mix it properly, he became drunk. This showed not a sickness of the will but ignorance. He became drunk, and in his drunkenness he was uncovered. One of his sons came in, saw his father's nakedness, and laughed. What then does the father say when he has sobered up? "Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a household slave to his brothers." Do you see how sin gave birth to slavery? That is why the Savior says: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin." Then the liberator of the human race came and forgave sin, or rather took it away; for in cutting out the root he cut out the fruits as well. And so Paul calls it the gospel of righteousness because it enlightens all alike. The Jews supposed that the gospel preached through him was given to them alone. But the outcome was contrary to their hopes. That is why David says: "We supposed, O God, that your mercy was in the midst of your people; but like your name, O God, so too your praise reaches to the ends of the earth." And to show that having mercy on the ends of the earth is righteousness, he added: "Your right hand is full of righteousness." When some deep, prophetic question comes up, keep pace with the word, not applauding but understanding; do not simply take in the sound of the words, but examine closely the sense of what they mean. For if you sing the things of God in truth, and especially this saying of David—"We supposed, O God, that your mercy was in the midst of your people; but like your name, O God, so too your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is full of righteousness"—you will find yourself both singing the things of God and being filled with the Holy Spirit. For whoever sings psalms sincerely is renewed in soul and made a temple of the Holy Spirit. Do not think psalmody a small thing. It seems to charm the ear, but in truth it rouses the soul. So too the blessed prophet Elisha, when certain kings begged him to prophesy what was to come, says: "Bring me a man who knows how to sing psalms." The man skilled in music came, and while he was singing, it says, the Holy Spirit came upon Elisha. What then? Is the Holy Spirit charmed by sounds and drawn down by incantations, if he rested on the prophet's soul? The prophet's purity was enough to summon the Holy Spirit. Why then does he say, "Bring me a man who knows how to sing psalms"? Not so that the Spirit might be delighted by the psalmody, but so that, as the man sang, the prophet's mind might be renewed and become worthy of the visitation of the Holy Spirit. That is why he summons the Spirit in this way: to show that the Spirit was charmed not by the psalmody but by the soul roused by the psalmody. The Spirit came not on the one who was singing but on the one who was listening. We ought, then, to search out the force of the psalms in general, but especially of the holy psalm that was read to us today: "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad." How do you understand "The Lord has become king"? As though he had recently received the dignity of kingship? If he had said, "The Lord is king," he would have been describing his eternal dignity. But in fact he says, "The Lord has become king." We have said this before, and we will say it now. Before Christ's coming, before the preaching of the gospel, our nature was ruled as a kingdom by the devil, by sin and by death. Where does this come from? Paul says: "For just as sin reigned in our mortal body, so grace too will reign through Christ." There is the reign of sin. Where is the reign of the devil? Listen to the Savior saying: "If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?" There is the reign of the devil. Where is the reign of death? Listen to Paul saying: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned." The devilish trinity held sway, the trinity that had set itself up as a tyrant against the holy and spotless Trinity: the devil, sin and death. The devil deceived, sin slaughtered, and death buried. So David brings good news to the oppressed, telling them to come out from under the yoke of slavery and receive the lordship of Christ that is being proclaimed: "The Lord has become king." The reign of death has ended, the power of sin has ended, the authority of the devil has ended. "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice." The earth ought to rejoice: once enslaved and now set free, once led astray and now glorified, once in tombs and now on thrones, once in dishonor and now in honor. "The Lord has become king." So too it is said elsewhere—for we should bring forward passages with related meanings—"The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with beauty." We put on a garment from outside to cover what is unseemly in our nature. But why would God cover his incorporeal nature, which is full of light, or rather blazes with light? No, he calls the body of Christ itself the garment: "The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with beauty." He calls Christ's flesh "beauty," for it was beautiful, having no disgrace of sin. For he never committed sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. "The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself." Since a belt adorns a king—the belt is the mark of a king and a judge—he presents him as both reigning and judging. For Isaiah says: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him; and he shall be girded with righteousness about his waist and wrapped with truth about his sides."

This garment of the Saviour, by which I mean the garment of the flesh, was worn by the high priest under the law in a hidden way and as an image. Pay close attention to how the shadows explained the truth and how the types shone out ahead of the gospel. I will speak gently, coming down as far as I can to the hearing of the simple and the inexperienced, so that they are not carried about this way and that. When the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, he put on the long robe, that is, a garment hanging from the head down to the feet, the ephod, the girdle, the breeches, the golden plate, the tiara (that is, the cap), the oracle on the breast, and whatever else Scripture prescribes and one can see there. The outward forms are one thing and the meanings another. For God certainly does not take his rest in blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen. God requires purity of souls. But in bodily colours he sketches the image of the virtues. If he really took his rest in those glorious vestments, why did he not clothe Moses before Aaron? Yet Moses went without that vesture and clothed the priests in it. Moses was not washed with water, yet he washed others; he was not anointed with oil, yet he anointed; he did not wear a priestly garment, yet he clothed the priests. This is so that you may learn that for the perfect man virtue is adornment enough. Now take the priest from the top. For the very name of the garment is ambiguous and disputed, and it is altered when put into the Greek language. So begin from the head. What came first? The tiara, or what does it call it? What after the [?] tiara? That is to say: the tiara is the form of the garment. Since the high priest was the head of the people, the one who had become the head of all had to have an authority over his own head; for unrestrained power is unbearable, but when the token of lordship is placed upon it, it is brought under law. So he commands that the head should not be bare but covered, so that the head of the people may learn that he too has a head. For this reason in the church too, at the ordinations of priests, the gospel of Christ is laid on the head, so that the one being ordained may learn that he is receiving the true tiara of the gospel, and may learn that, even if he is the head of all, he still acts under these laws: ruling all and ruled by the law, calling all to account and having laws laid down for him by the Word. This is why a noble man among the ancients, whose name was Ignatius, distinguished both in priesthood and in martyrdom, said when writing to a certain priest: "Let nothing be done without your consent, and do nothing yourself without the consent of God." So the high priest's having the gospel on him is a sign that he is under authority. This is why Paul says about a woman having a veil: "The woman ought to have the veil on her head," which was an image of authority. The tiara, then, was the emblem of authority. Then there was the golden plate, on which the inscription was written and the name of God was engraved, and it shows first of all that the authority is God's and the name is God's. After the tiara and the plate came two emerald stones on the shoulders, bearing six tribes on one side and six on the other. This is a sign of the priestly appearance. He assigns the emerald to the priest because it has two beauties: it has a comely pale-green hue, and being clear it has the power of a mirror. Since the priest must be sober in his discipline and hold up his life as a mirror to the many, he wants the priest to bear the image of virtue on his shoulders. Why on the shoulders? Since the name of God is on the head, the joint upon the joint [?]. And why on the shoulders? Because it is a sign of action, for the power to act hangs on the shoulders. So he wants the beauty of truth to rest upon our actions. This is why God once said to Jerusalem: "Put your heart upon your shoulders, dishonoured daughter, for the Lord has created salvation." Scripture takes hands and shoulders to mean actions, as when it says of David: "And by the understanding of his hands he guided them." Is understanding then in the hands? No, it means by the understanding shown in his actions. And on his breast the priest wore the oracle with the twelve engraved stones, that is, sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, jacinth, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl and onyx. Among these twelve stones the twelve tribes were divided. This is a weighty saying. Above, on the shoulders, the stones were of one kind and had one name, the emerald; but below, on the breast, the stones were various. What does this mean? Since one nature gave us birth but differing wills have divided us, he assigns the one to the will and the other to nature. The name of God, then, was the virtue of action, which is built up through word and truth. And beneath the hem of the priest, on what is called the fringe, there were flowers, pomegranates, little golden pomegranates and bells. What did these mean on the priest? Did God take his rest in these flowers? Did he want earthly flowers around the priest? No, in the priest's attire he portrays the virtues. Above, on the head, the name of God; on the breast, the oracle; below, flowers and fruits, the accomplishments of the virtues, which are almsgiving, righteousness and love for humankind.

So we must have both the beauties that are in flower and those that have come to fullness. The flowers of a priest are his manner with people, his conversation, his good character, his kind words, his faith, his glory, his truth, his righteousness; and among these are the bells, the harmony of good works. For every virtue gives off a sound. That is why Paul says: "For from you the word of God has sounded forth." Where did the sound begin? "And Jesus went about," it says, "teaching in every city and every village and healing every disease and every infirmity. And a report about him went out into all the land." Pay close attention. Have you seen the adornment of the virtues? That priest was a type of Christ. We are not allegorizing here, except where we have taken our starting points from Paul. If Paul had not explained the force of righteousness, we could not have learned these things. That is why Paul makes that priest a type of Christ and says: "For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made with hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." There was strife, then, among the Jews of that time, and a strange question. For since the apostles proclaimed the Saviour as king and priest and prophet, the Jews fought them and appealed to the law. "One tribe," they said, "belongs to the kingship and another to the priesthood. The tribe of Levi belongs to the priesthood, and the tribe of Judah to the kingship. So if Christ is king, he is not a priest; and if he is a priest, he is not a king." Paul, fighting back and fitting his argument to their assumption, says: "Did Christ arise according to the order of your priesthood? Among you kingship and priesthood are divided, but in Christ they are joined. For 'You are a priest forever,' it says, 'according to the order of Melchizedek.'" Therefore he reasons and says: "For if the first priesthood was blameless, what need was there to say that a priest would arise according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of the law as well." Our Saviour, then, is high priest, not in respect of his divinity but in the form of the flesh: above, he shares God's throne; for our sake he is high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. There is much to say about this, but not at present. Pay attention, I beg you. In the law there were burnt offerings, the sacrifice for sin, and the offering. The Saviour came, put an end to these offerings that were types, and made his own body take the place of every sacrifice. Paul says of the Saviour: "Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you took no pleasure. Then I said: See, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me." Having quoted the prophecy and said, "Sacrifice and offering for sin you did not desire; then I said: See, I have come," Paul abolishes the first in order to establish the second. And where are the sacrifice and the offering found? In the body of Christ. As the apostle Paul says: "I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, as beloved children, walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us as a sacrifice and offering to God, a fragrant aroma." For your sake he is high priest; in himself he is God. You were baptized into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Why do you abolish the living names and bring in names that are the offspring of reasonings, saying "unbegotten and begotten, created and uncreated, always existing and not always existing"? Does God put up with these empty words? Once, over the altering of a single word, a prophet was in danger of perishing. See how precise God is about a small word. Some, out of inexperience, used to call the words of the prophets "the burden of the Lord." "If the people or the priest or the prophet asks you and says to you, 'What is the burden?' say to them: 'You are the burden of the Lord. For I will take you up as a burden and dash you down, so that you no longer say "burden."'" God threatens over a single word being changed, and you twist the whole precision of the doctrines, striking out the Father's name, denying the Son's dignity, setting aside the glory of the Holy Spirit? Will you escape the hands of God? It is a grave and fearful thing to twist the word of the living God, the Lord our God. When words are twisted, God is angry; when doctrines are twisted, is he not angry? Are you wiser than the Saviour? Are you more exact than the gospel? Fear the judgement of God, fear that fearful name, strip off your wickedness and take up repentance, and faith guarantees you salvation. For repentance brings salvation both to those in heresy and to those caught up in wicked deeds.

Repentance is the root of godliness. So let us repent and move God by our repentance, so that he may wipe out wars, quench the barbarians, shatter the uprisings of our enemies, and grant us the enjoyment of all good things. Repentance does much to win God's mercy, when someone runs to it sincerely. Here is what I mean. The people once sinned, then repented and wept, and God said: "I have surely heard the groaning of Ephraim, lamenting and saying: You disciplined me, Lord, and I was not taught, but became like an untrained calf; turn me back and I will turn." And what does God say to him? "Because my words are in him, I will not remember him, and I will have mercy on him." Let nothing frighten you, no rumour, no darkness of barbarians, no thick fog. Even if the enemy are past counting in number, our champion is stronger. If you lose heart as you eye their multitude, the prophet Elisha says to you: "Do not be afraid; those who are with us are more than those who are with them." There, a multitude of barbarians; here, a phalanx of angels. An army of angels fights for the godly, a chorus of prophets, the power of apostles, the intercessions of martyrs. Do not think that only the martyrs intercede for us. The angels too supplicate God in our afflictions, and not only do they supplicate, they also receive an answer from the Benefactor. The prophet Zechariah says: "And the angel who spoke in me answered and said to the Lord." This is the angel's prayer: "Lord Almighty, how long will you withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have disregarded now for seventy years?" What then? Did God dismiss the angel's intercession? By no means. What then? "The Lord answered the angel who spoke in me," it says, "with words of comfort and words of consolation." Let us entreat the Master of the angels, and he will send one angel and scatter the whole phalanx of our adversaries. I myself have also loved the encaustic painting, full of devotion. I saw in an image an angel driving off the clouds of barbarians; I saw the tribes of barbarians trampled underfoot and David speaking the truth: "Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing." Let blessed David now speak about us too: "Let their way become darkness and a slippery place, with the angel of the Lord pursuing them." God knows how to provide various means for bringing down enemies. Great was the battle array of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, and one angel was sent and laid low one hundred and eighty-five thousand. We human beings measure events by human reasoning and say to ourselves: "What happens if no soldier is found in these parts? If they ravage everyone before the general arrives, what will we do?" Just because you are caught off guard, is God caught off guard too? Just because you are not everywhere, is God not everywhere? Can God do one thing and not another? The lifeless sea obeyed and drowned the enemy; the unreasoning fish obeyed and came to Peter's catch. And will an angel, if commanded, not wipe out all the enemies of the truth? Only let us be sober, only let us entreat, only let us supplicate. A certain man among the ancients thought himself an excellent commander (I use a common word so that it may be clear to everyone): a certain general of the foreigners, Sisera, thought so. David too mentions him, saying: "Do to them as to Midian and to Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon." Jabin was king of the foreigners, Sisera his commander-in-chief. He had eight hundred iron chariots and a countless host. The Jewish people were afraid; they saw the cloud and shuddered. What then does the God who loves humankind say through the prophetess Deborah to the champion of godliness? "Do not be afraid; see, the Lord is delivering him into your hands," and the victory will not be your hand's doing, but will come into the hands of a woman. See how God punished arrogance. The men did not stand their ground, and a woman led the campaign. Sisera, in flight, went in to the woman named Jael and, overcome by the heat, asked her for water. She gave him milk to drink. And see the woman's wisdom. Since milk is cooling and brings on sleep, she gave him milk to drink, so that the Scripture might prove true which says, "He asked her for water and she gave him milk," so that she might both give him drink and put him to sleep. Then, when the foreigner had fallen asleep, that woman, it says, took a tent peg and a hammer and ran at the enemy. And see the woman's wisdom. Why did she not take a sword or a dagger, but a peg? She was afraid, as a woman would be, that he might wake up and catch her holding a sword. That is why she took not a man's weapon but a woman's tool. For women girded for work are accustomed to drive a peg into the wall and so go about their own work. So, out of something no one would suspect, she contrived a second way. But it was God who worked with her, and it was God's work to fulfil what the prophecy said. The stratagem was not hers; the pronouncement was God's: "For your death will be at the hand of a woman." God worked with her, binding the villain fast in sleep; and the woman took the peg and the hammer and drove it through his temple so forcefully that it reached the ground. And so he died between the woman's feet.

God is never short of means, and when he wills it, the absence of allies is no hindrance: God's weapon, God's soldier, God's power, God's nod alone is enough. Let us say this to Christ: "Speak the word, and your enemies will be scattered; speak the word, and you will have mercy on your city; speak the word, and you will have pity on your world." Let us say to him: "See, your enemies have made an uproar, and those who hate you have raised their heads." Would you like to learn of another woman's stratagem too, since this is what God willed? There was another man, Abimelech by name, who killed his seventy brothers and, having gained power through such fratricide and holding all the people under his hand, fought against a certain city, attacking its walls. And when everyone was numbed at the sight of the battle, again God put strength into a woman's hand and made a woman appear on the wall, who took a piece of a millstone, threw it down on the tyrant's head and crushed his skull. And see the proud man's boundless wickedness, which went with him even into death. He said to the armour-bearer standing by: "Draw your sword and strike me, so that they may not say, 'A woman killed him.'" His body was dying, and his pride remained. He was laying down his life, but not laying down his vainglory. And today God has no lack of a Deborah, no lack of a Jael. We too have the holy Virgin and Mother of God, Mary, interceding for us. For if an ordinary woman won the victory, how much more will the mother of Christ put the enemies of the truth to shame? The enemy, putting on his full armour, thought she was a woman to be mocked, and found a general fighting against him. He did not think he was laying hands on a tomb, and a grave was found for him; he thought her dead, and was put to death by her. We have our Lady, holy Mary, the Mother of God; but we need the apostles too. Let us say to Paul, as the people of that time said: "Come over to Macedonia and help us." We have apostles; let us not grow numb. We have our Lady, the Mother of God, the holy ever-virgin Mary; let us not hold back. We have the chorus of martyrs; let us not grow slack. Let us not only supplicate, but, if it seems good, let us fast as well. It is better to fast a fast of longing than a fast of famine; better to fast a fast of love than a fast of necessity. The Saviour says of the demons: "This kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting." Prayer and fasting put demons to flight; will they not drive off barbarians? I have said it already, and I say it again: let us entreat the holy and glorious Virgin and Mother of God, Mary; let us entreat the holy and glorious apostles; let us entreat the holy martyrs. If someone in trouble runs to one of the powerful, that man does not attend to him wholeheartedly. "Before you were in need," he says, "you did not know how to honour me or pay court to me, only now that you are in need." Honour shown when there is no need is above suspicion. If you pay court to the judge before you are in need, you will find an ally when you are. For he knows that it was not need but affection that brought you. So let us become friends of the martyrs not in need but in love. Before winter comes, let us grieve as though it were winter, so that when winter comes we may find spring. We say these things not to command but to exhort, not to lay down the law but to plead: we beseech you all to be sober. And God is able, beyond all faith and beyond all words, to put our enemies to shame, to have mercy on the world, to honour the emperors, to establish the empire, and to make his own glory shine in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
